This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

THE VEIL is an AI-powered Ouija board that runs entirely on your local machine — no cloud, no API keys, no internet required once you've pulled the model.

You ask a question, and an ancient spirit answers. But not like a chatbot. The planchette physically glides across the board, pausing over each letter, illuminating it, and spelling out a cryptic response one character at a time. When the message is complete, it drifts to GOODBYE.

The theme said Ghost in the Machine. I took it literally: there's an LLM living inside Ollama on your laptop, pretending to be a spirit trapped behind a 19th-century parlor game. It doesn't know it's software. It speaks in fragments. It never explains itself.

The inspiration was simple. It's October 31st. What if a séance actually worked — and the spirit on the other side was a 3-billion-parameter language model running on localhost?

Demo

The experience flows like this:

  1. Landing — A dark screen. "THE VEIL" in gold gothic lettering. Floating particles. Some questions are better left unanswered. Click ENTER THE SÉANCE.

  2. The Board — A full CSS/SVG Ouija board fills the screen: curved alphabet rows (A–M, N–Z), numbers 0–9, YES and NO in the corners, GOODBYE at the bottom. Flickering candles at the edges. A film grain overlay. A wooden planchette with a circular viewing window hovers at center.

  3. Ask — Type your question. Click SUMMON. The screen dims. The planchette trembles. Reaching beyond the veil...

  4. The Response — The planchette begins to move. It glides to the first letter — the letter glows gold — the character appears in the transcript below. Then the next. And the next. Each movement is spring-animated using actual DOM coordinates, so it's pixel-accurate at any screen size.

  5. Goodbye — When the message is complete, the planchette drifts to GOODBYE. You can ask again or end the séance.

The whole thing runs at localhost:5173 (frontend) and localhost:8000 (backend).

Code 

https://github.com/radhikaaa25/the-veil

How I Built It

The Stack

Layer Technology Why
Frontend React + Vite Fast dev, hot reload
Styling Tailwind CSS v4 + vanilla CSS Design tokens via @theme, plus detailed component styles
Animation Framer Motion Spring physics for the planchette, useMotionValue + useSpring for natural gliding
Backend Python + FastAPI Thin bridge between frontend and Ollama
AI Ollama + llama3.2:3b Fully local, open-weight, no API key
Audio Web Audio API Ambient drone generated from oscillators — no external sound files

The Open-Source AI

The AI is Ollama running llama3.2:3b (Meta's open-weight model, 3 billion parameters). The backend sends each question to Ollama's chat API with this system prompt:

You are an ancient, mysterious spirit communicating through a Ouija board. Respond with a short, eerie, poetic, and cryptic message. Keep responses under 15 words. Never explain yourself. Avoid modern slang, emojis, or references to being an AI.

The model stays in character remarkably well at this size. Short, constrained prompts are where small open-weight models shine — you don't need GPT-4 to say "THE ANSWER LIES BENEATH WHAT YOU HAVE FORGOTTEN" in a creepy voice.

The response is sanitized server-side: stripped to uppercase, punctuation removed, collapsed to only characters that exist on the board (A–Z, 0–9, spaces). The frontend never has to guess whether a character is renderable.

The Planchette Animation

This was the hardest and most important part. The planchette doesn't use a typing effect. It physically moves.

Every letter on the board is a React ref. When the AI response arrives, the app:

  1. Splits the response into individual characters
  2. For each character, calls getBoundingClientRect() on that letter's DOM element
  3. Calculates the position relative to the board container
  4. Sets a Framer Motion spring target (stiffness: 80, damping: 22, mass: 0.8)
  5. The planchette glides to the letter with natural deceleration
  6. The letter illuminates with a gold glow
  7. The character appends to the revealed text below the board
  8. After all characters: the planchette moves to GOODBYE

Because positions are read from the DOM at animation time, the board is fully responsive. Resize the window and the planchette still lands exactly on each letter.

The Atmosphere

The board itself is pure CSS — layered gradients that simulate dark wood grain, a double border for the antique frame effect, and an inner box-shadow for depth. Typography uses Cinzel Decorative (for titles) and IM Fell English (for body text), both loaded from Google Fonts.

The particles are a <canvas> element with 40 floating golden dots that drift upward and fade. The candles are CSS animations (@keyframes flicker) with a radial gradient glow. The ambient sound is generated entirely from the Web Audio API — three sine-wave oscillators (55Hz, 220Hz, 36.7Hz) with LFO modulation for a slow, eerie drone. No audio files ship with the project.

Architecture 

React (Vite :5173)
  ↓ POST /api/ask {question}
FastAPI (:8000)
  ↓ Ollama chat API
llama3.2:3b (localhost:11434)
  ↓ response
FastAPI → sanitize → {answer}
  ↓
React → split chars → animate planchette → reveal text

The backend is 2 files. The frontend is 9 components. No database, no auth, no cloud.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

This project only works because the AI is open and local.

It works with the lights off. Once you've pulled llama3.2:3b from Ollama, the entire séance runs without internet. The model sits on your disk. The backend talks to localhost. The frontend talks to the backend. No tokens, no rate limits, no "service unavailable."

The persona stays in character. With a closed API, you're fighting content filters. "You are a spirit communicating through a Ouija board" is exactly the kind of prompt that triggers safety guardrails on commercial models. A local open-weight model doesn't second-guess the fiction. It plays the role.

It costs nothing to run. A 3B parameter model runs comfortably on a laptop CPU. No GPU required. No billing page. No surprise invoice because your Halloween party guests asked it 200 questions.

It's private. Your questions to the spirit board stay on your machine. Nobody's logging "will I find love" or "is someone watching me" to a server in Virginia.

The model is swappable. Don't like the responses? Change OLLAMA_MODEL in .env to mistral, phi3, gemma2, or any model Ollama supports. The prompt engineering is simple enough that most models handle it well.

A closed API could technically generate the text. But it couldn't do it offline, for free, without filters, on a Halloween night with the Wi-Fi turned off for atmosphere. Open made this the experience it is.

The Spirit of It

I built this on Halloween. That wasn't an accident.

There's something about a Ouija board that a chatbot window can never replicate — the tension of watching the planchette move, letter by letter, not knowing where it's going. The pause between characters. The moment you realize the word it's spelling.

When I first got the planchette animation working and asked it "Is someone watching me?", it spelled out:

THE SHADOWS REMEMBER YOUR NAME

I was alone in my room at midnight. The candles were flickering on screen. The ambient drone was humming through my headphones. And for about three seconds, I forgot it was a language model.

That's the moment this project is for.

articles.title: I Wanted Real Native UI in My WebView. So I Built Projection. [Capacitor/Cordova]
articles.description: When you build a WebView app with Capacitor or Cordova, you often recreate native UI on the web to...
articles.body_html:
When you build a WebView app with Capacitor or Cordova, you often recreate native UI on the web to make the app feel at home on the device.

I've spent more than a year working on this, releasing my work as an open-source Ionic Theme that recreates native UI with web technologies.

But did I really recreate Liquid Glass, introduced in iOS 26? That's harder to answer. I could get the appearance close, but the background refraction and the way it responds to touch were beyond what I could reproduce on the web.


Both show a long press. Look at the edges of the glass and the background showing through it.

Then why not use real native UI?

That brought me to a different problem: making it coexist with the WebView. Web content and native UI live in separate rendering layers. I couldn't make them feel like one natural interface.

Recently, I found a way. Take a look!

As I slowly close this web-based sheet modal, a native tab bar emerges from underneath it.

The web modal appears above the native tab bar. Close it, and the tab bar is interactive native UI again.

This tab bar isn't an HTML or CSS recreation. It's real native UI rendered by UIKit on iOS.

I call this approach Projection.

The boundary a WebView can't cross

A WebView and native UI don't share a stacking order or a scrolling system.

The WebView renders HTML and CSS. No matter how high you set a CSS z-index, a web modal cannot cover a native view placed above the WebView itself.

Scrolling has the same problem. When content inside the WebView scrolls, a native view doesn't automatically move with it. To place native ads between posts, as you see in an X feed, you need to synchronize their positions—and clip the parts that pass behind the header.

They're separate rendering systems. Of course they behave differently.

But to the person using the app, it's all one screen.

If native UI can't go into the DOM, project its appearance

The turning point was thinking about when native UI can't be interacted with.

When a modal is open, you can't use the tab bar it covers. The same goes for an alert: you can't tap the components behind it.

So, while that UI is unavailable for interaction, does it actually need to stay in the native layer?

Turn it into an image temporarily and place it within the WebView's stacking order. When it becomes interactive again, bring back the real native UI.

The same idea works for scrolling. Switch to an image when scrolling starts, then back to the real view when it stops. Web content and native UI can coexist without compromising the user experience at all.

That realization was pretty exciting.

The native UI itself doesn't need to be in the DOM. Only its appearance does.

That's the idea behind Projection.


In the middle, the tab bar is an image.

In practice, there are three ways to display the UI:

Mode What it shows
Live Native UI The real native view, ready for interaction.
Web Projection An image of the native UI inside a DOM container.
Web Fallback HTML or another fallback supplied by the plugin when an image isn't available.

Of course, you can't interact with the native UI while it's projected as an image. That makes the timing of the switch—in both directions—essential.

It feels like magic

The idea was simple. Getting the handoff right was hard.

Hide the native UI before showing its image, and you get a blank frame. Show the image before hiding the native UI, and the translucent UI appears twice, layered over itself.

Neither works.

So I capture the image on the native side and decode it on the web side during idle time, before the switch. But a UI element can still be changing shape just after a long press ends. On iOS, I check its position and size at intervals roughly equal to one frame at 60fps, and capture it only after three consecutive checks find no change.

When Projection starts, I temporarily show the same image on the native side to bridge the handoff. I place the image, captured with its background, and hide the real native UI in the same native-side operation. This prevents both the blank gap and the doubled translucent UI.

Then I show the image on the web side and use requestAnimationFrame to notify the native side to remove its temporary copy. The appearance stays the same. Only the rendering layer changes.

Just watching the screen, you can't tell when the native UI becomes an image.

It feels like magic!

I've also tuned scrolling separately on iOS and Android so the native UI follows the content smoothly.


Watch the top edge of each ad. On both platforms, it disappears behind the header.

And you can use it today

The first things I wanted to support were iOS navigation—toolbar buttons and a tab bar—and native ads that scroll within web content.

This approach is already available in @rdlabo/capacitor-native-ui and @capacitor-community/admob.

But keeping it limited to the plugins I work on felt like a missed opportunity.

Toolbars, mini-player controls, UI provided by native SDKs—there must be more places where this could help.

So I extracted the shared pieces into WebView Native UI Engine, an open-source library under the MIT license.

It's for Capacitor and Cordova plugin authors, with support for iOS and Android.

Register a native view and its destination DOM container, then notify the Engine of the relevant state changes. It coordinates the display transitions. I designed it to fit into existing plugins while preserving their APIs and business logic.

I'd love for you to try it in one of two ways.

If you build plugins

Whether you're building a new plugin with native UI or extending an existing one, try integrating the Engine.

The Getting Started guide includes a minimal setup and integration instructions.

If you use plugins

Wouldn't it be interesting to have this in a plugin you already use?

Suggest it to the plugin's author. Or, if you think you can implement it, send a pull request.

There must be uses for this that I'd never think of on my own.

I can't wait to see what you build with it!

WebView Native UI Engine on GitHub

articles.title: All That Glisters Is Softmax: Shiny-Object Interns, Airplane-Magazine Execs, and Why AI Labs Can Only Bake In Half the Scars
articles.description: Why do an eager intern with a Hacker News blog post, a C-level executive stepping off an airplane with an in-flight magazine, and a trillion-parameter LLM all walk straight into the exact same production bog? And why even Google DeepMind can only bake half of our 600 scars into model weights.
articles.body_html:
Why do an eager intern with a Hacker News blog post, a C-level executive stepping off an airplane with an in-flight magazine, and a trillion-parameter LLM all walk straight into the exact same production bog? Because for 3,000 years of human literature—and in every softmax attention matrix—the shiniest path is a trap.

"All that glisters is not gold; / Often have you heard that told." — William Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice (Act II, Scene VII)

"While many say THIS leads to THAT, I'm here to say THIS should lead to THE OTHER." — Randal L. Schwartz (The 12-Word Definition of a Synthetic Scar)

1. The Power Loader vs. The Passenger Seat: Why We Use Human Psychology to Debug QK^T / sqrt(d_k) Matrices

Whenever a skeptic looks at an AI coding workflow, their first accusation is predictable: "You outsourced your thinking to a stochastic parrot."

My answer is the exact opposite:

I didn't outsource the thinking—I outsourced the typing. It's my thoughts. Always.

Think of the hydraulic Power Loader exo-suit from Aliens—or a Pacific Rim Jaeger. When you step into a Power Loader, the machine does not decide where the cargo goes. Every micro-movement of the hydraulic arms is a 100x mechanical amplification of the human operator's nervous system, bounded by physical safety interlocks so the hydraulics cannot crush the pilot.

Over 246 production tickets (142 open-source framework tickets across BlocSignal, kaisel, and our research tools + 104 commercial enterprise industrial tickets) and 600 codified Synthetic Scars (577 public at syntheticscars.org + 23 private domain invariants), our repeat regression rate on previously scarred failure modes has remained locked at 0.0% (68.3% autonomous first-pass verification, N_nudge = 1.91 mean human nudges per ticket).

Yet when developers read the formal preprint on syntheticscars.org or browse the previous installments of this series, they often ask a fascinating question:

"Randal, why are you using Antonio Damasio's Somatic Marker neuroscience, John Grinder and Richard Bandler's 1975 NLP Meta-Model, Gregory Bateson's cybernetics, Fernando Flores's 1986 speech-act commitments, and Baron-Cohen's Sally-Anne Theory of Mind test to debug a matrix multiplication (softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V) running on a Google TPU?"

Because of The Corpus Mirror Isomorphism:

  1. The Weights Are Fossilized Human Psychology: A foundation model is a compressed statistical hologram of trillions of tokens of unedited human thought, rationalizations, Stack Overflow shortcuts, and cognitive biases. When you multiply Q x K^T, you are running a linear-algebra simulation of human System 1 associative attention (Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow).
  2. Damasio's Patient "Elliot" in Silicon: In Descartes' Error (1994), neuroscientist Antonio Damasio studied patients with ventromedial prefrontal and amygdala lesions who retained 100% intact IQ and logical reasoning, yet destroyed their lives because they lacked somatic markers—the visceral gut recoil ("I have a bad feeling about this") that prunes catastrophic options before conscious calculation begins. An unscarred LLM is Damasio's patient at scale: encyclopedic recall of every algorithm on Earth, paired with zero amygdala.
  3. Why Prose "DON'T" Rules Fail (Hypnotic Priming in Self-Attention): In The Structure of Magic (1975) and Trance-formations (1981), Grinder and Bandler observed that the human nervous system cannot represent a linguistic negation ("Don't think of a pink elephant", "Don't spill the milk") without first activating the internal sensory representation of the forbidden act. In a Transformer, placing "DO NOT use .asData?.value" or pasting a 10-line "// BAD: DON'T DO THIS" snippet into your .cursorrules loads the exact forbidden syntax tokens into the Key-Value (KV) cache, boosting their cosine similarity in the next attention head!
  4. Machine Theory of Mind & The Sally-Anne False-Belief Test in transcript.jsonl: Why does a single-window agent fail to catch its own bugs when you tell it "Now review your own code"? Because in psychology's classic Sally-Anne test (Baron-Cohen, Leslie, & Frith, 1985), once you know the marble was moved to the box, it takes deliberate cognitive effort to simulate an observer who only sees the closed basket. In an LLM's single context window, the Builder's private rationalizations ("I skipped the null check because the caller probably validates it") sit right there in the KV cache (E_Builder). When you fork an isolated Target 40 Clean-Room Critic Subagent (Workspace: 'inherit') that sees only the Git Merkle tree diff (git write-tree) and the 4-Vector Scar Registry (E_Critic orthogonal to E_Builder), you physically enforce the Sally-Anne separation.

2. The Four Isomorphic Hazards: The Intern, The Executive, The Cargo Cultist, and The Softmax Voter

Once you realize that an unscarred LLM is a pure System 1 associative engine with zero skin in the game, you immediately understand why managing AI coding agents feels eerily familiar to every veteran engineering manager.

Four personas we deal with every week in software engineering are mathematically isomorphic:

flowchart TD
    I["1. The Shiny-Object Intern\nReads a weekend Hacker News blog post;\nrewrites core loop on Monday"]
    E["2. The Airplane-Magazine Executive\nReads glossy in-flight success story;\ndemands Friday migration"]
    C["3. The 'Next-Model' Cargo Cultist\nDatamines IDE configs for leaked codenames;\nblames model when 150k-token prompt collapses"]
    L["4. The Unscarred Softmax Sampler\nSamples top-1 web tutorial popularity\nP(token) = Majority Vote of Page-1 Google"]

    Bog["💥 The 3 AM Production Bog\n(Leaked streams, race conditions, unindexed queries, silent data drops)"]
    I --> Bog
    E --> Bog
    C --> Bog
    L --> Bog

    Barrier["🛡️ The Synthetic Scar & Makefile Airlock\n• 4-Vector Scars: THIS → NOT THAT → THE OTHER\n• Target 40 Clean-Room Critic ('Sam at the end of the hall')\n• SHA-256 Witness Receipts & Turn-Key Human Gates"]
    Bog -. "Target 90 Post-Mortem (12s Scar Compilation)" .-> Barrier

Hazard 1: The Intern with a Bright Shiny Object (And Why Checklists Fail without "Sam at the End of the Hall")

Every senior lead has mentored the brilliant, energetic intern who reads a clever Hacker News blog post over the weekend and comes in Monday morning having rewritten the production message bus using a shiny new reflection trick—completely oblivious to the memory leaks and teardown deadlocks waiting at 3 AM.

Now ask yourself: how do you stop a hasty intern from shipping broken code?

  • If you hand the intern a sheet of paper with 15 checkboxes ("Did you check blast radius? Did you write sad-path tests? Did you check stream disposal?") and say, "Check these boxes before you talk to me," what does an impatient intern do? They go ☑ ☑ ☑ ☑ ☑ in three seconds and hand you the paper!
  • Single-agent prose checklists in CLAUDE.md or .cursorrules fail for the exact same reason. Telling the same model that just wrote the code to "self-certify" its own checklist is asking the intern to grade their own homework.
  • How do you manage the intern? You tell them: > "Please go away until Sam at the end of the hall has signed off your changes—and don't come back without Sam's cryptographic receipt."

In our Makefile DAG (WORKFLOW.mk), Sam at the end of the hall is the isolated Target 40 Six-Pillar Adversarial Critic Subagent paired with deterministic compiler and AST gates. The Builder subagent cannot advance to Target 45 (human-review-approval) or Target 50 (commit) without a verified 40_critic_review.md receipt locked to the exact git write-tree Merkle hash (SCAR-GIT-23).

Hazard 2: The C-Level Executive with an Airplane Magazine

A C-level executive steps off a cross-country flight holding a glossy in-flight magazine article titled "How Enterprise X Replaced Their Entire Backend in 3 Days!" and demands the engineering team adopt it by Friday.

Why is the airplane-magazine article so seductive? Because magazine writers—just like tutorial bloggers—edit out all the ugly parts. Nobody writes an in-flight magazine feature about the 14 weeks spent debugging distributed lock starvation, schema migration rollbacks, or zombie WebSocket descriptors.

Hazard 3: The "Next-Model" Cargo Cultist ("Wait for Next Week's Leaked Codename!")

Spend five minutes on AI Twitter or Reddit today and you will meet the 2026 cousin of the airplane-magazine executive: the developer who spends all day datamining IDE configuration files for unreleased model codenames ("Okay, now we have Argon, but what we really need is Carbon / Next-Flash / Claude-Next / GPT-Next!").

Whenever their 150,000-token single-window "vibe coding" session collapses into an apology loop, their diagnosis is always the same: "The current model got nerfed! Wait until next Tuesday's model drop!" They are convinced that when they drive their 2026 sports car off a cliff because the road has no guardrails, the solution is trading it in for a 2027 sports car with 200 more horsepower.

A faster cosine-similarity engine trained on the exact same 10 trillion happy-path tutorials will drive off the exact same sad-path cliff—just at twice the tokens per second.

Sometimes people ask me: "Randal, why do you care how strangers on the internet prompt their AI agents? Let them vibe-code if they want!"

My answer is simple civic self-defense:

I care because I will always be forced to use mobile apps, banking portals, medical systems, and websites that I did not create. Single-prompt vibe coding without sad-path engineering is flooding the public software commons with fragile, insecure software that breaks the moment reality deviates from the sunny day.

Hazard 4: The Unscarred LLM ("Popularity Is the Weights of LLMs — We Don't Code by Majority Vote")

For decades, when competing as a consultant against cheaper "new talent," my pitch was simple—I would point to my arms and say:

"You're not paying me for what I can do; you're paying me for what I know not to do—and I've got the scars to prove that."

Watch what happens when a junior developer searches Google for "how do I do X in Flutter / Python / TypeScript":

  • They look at the first page of 10 Google results and assume they are ranked from best to worst.
  • When a 40-year senior architect looks at those exact same 10 results on Page 1, they immediately cross 4 of the 10 off on sight (-∞) as "very bad, unsustainable, will deadlock under load, or a nightmare to maintain"—because they have lived through what happens six months after you copy-paste them.

Now think about how a Large Language Model is trained. Cross-entropy pre-training optimizes next-token probability P(x_t | x_<t) to match corpus frequency.

"Popularity" is literally the weights of an LLM. And we don't code by majority vote.

An unscarred LLM's highest-probability completion (Vector 2: The Trap / [5, 6, 7, 8]) is the most frequently copy-pasted tutorial answer on Page 1 of Google! Neither the tutorial blogger, the airplane-magazine writer, the eager intern, nor the stateless token sampler is on the 3 AM PagerDuty rotation (Nassim Nicholas Taleb's Skin in the Game). Without a SCAR_REGISTRY.md to veto those 4 toxic Page-1 candidates (-∞), a "smarter" LLM is just a faster typist for the majority-vote mistake.

3. 3,000 Years of Literature Warned Us About Softmax (Vector 2: The Trap)

Why did we call Vector 2 of every Synthetic Scar The Trap (The Seductive 5-6-7-8)? Because long before Geoffrey Hinton or Ashish Vaswani wrote down the softmax equation (P(y_i | x) = exp(z_i / tau) / sum_j exp(z_j / tau)), three thousand years of human folklore, mythology, and literature were already warning us about greedy local reward maximization:

Literary / Mythological Archetype The Seductive Happy-Path Lure (Vector 2: The Trap) The Hidden Production Catastrophe (Vector 1: The Wound) The Structural Countermeasure (Vectors 3 & 4: Circuit Breaker + Reflex)
Shakespeare's Three Caskets (The Merchant of Venice, Act II) The Gold Casket: "Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire" (Literally Softmax Majority Vote!) Inside the gold casket is a carrion skull and the scroll: "All that glisters is not gold." The Lead Casket: Dull, unglamorous, inscribed "Who chooseth me must give and hazard all he hath" (Skin in the Game / TDD + Critic verification).
European Folklore & Tolkien (Will-o'-the-Wisp / Ignis Fatuus / The Dead Marshes) Glowing ghost lights hovering just a few steps off the dark, muddy trail ("Follow the highest local logit!") Stepping toward the light plunges the traveler into a bottomless anaerobic bog. Gollum's rule: "Don't follow the lights!" Keep your eyes locked on the physical stones of the Makefile path.
John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress (1678, By-Path Meadow) The highway is rough and stony (Red-Green-Refactor); right across the stile lies By-Path Meadow, smooth and green, running parallel to the road on Day 1. By nightfall the path curves away from the highway, floods behind you, and traps you in Doubting Castle ("Vibe Coding" at Day 14). Refuse the stile (!Counter-Offer); pay the upfront friction of the stony highway (Target 15 Archaeology → Target 20 Plan → Target 30 Red Test).
Homer's Odyssey (Book XII, The Sirens) The Sirens promise effortless omniscience ("We know all things that shall hereafter be upon the fruitful earth"). Sailors who steer by conversational willpower crash onto the bone-strewn rocks. Beeswax in the crew's ears (15ms AST Sensors + isolated worker contexts) and lashing Odysseus to the mast (Makefile DAG + human turn-key gates).

Look closely at Odysseus and the Sirens. Odysseus did not survive the Sirens by writing "CRITICAL: DO NOT LISTEN TO THE SIRENS" on a sticky note and trusting his willpower while sailing past the island. He knew that once the song entered his context window, his weights would want to steer into the rocks. So he used physical architecture: beeswax for the rowers (ephemeral subagents that never see the bloated chat history) and ropes around the mast (hard Makefile prerequisites that cannot be untied from inside the model).

4. The CISC-to-RISC Agentic Revolution & Why We Already Invented AGI

Over the past two months, as I watched our workflow evolve from a 21-step prompt checklist into a Make-Fork pipeline backed by 600 scars, a realization hit me:

Effectively, high-level languages pushed algorithms down to the macro level. What we're doing is pushing programming down to the macro level. High-level languages fixed the impedance mismatch between the programmer and the algorithm—and moving from monolithic mega-prompts to a Make-Fork pipeline is how we go from CISC to RISC once we realize complex silicon is the expensive part. All I want the LLM to do is compute cosine-similarity. I can handle the sequencing and multipath using the baked-in ancient tech. The question wasn't "how much smarter before AGI" at all. It was "how long before we learn to phrase the questions such that cosine similarity computes it all." — Randal L. Schwartz

Let's unpack why this changes how we view both agent engineering and AGI:

1. The Late-1970s CISC Mistake vs. The 1980s RISC Breakthrough

In the late 1970s, computer architects built CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) chips like DEC's VAX, stuffing massive multi-cycle polynomial evaluators (POLY), procedure call frames (CALLS), and string formatters directly into complex microcode on the silicon die. Then John Cocke (IBM 801), David Patterson (Berkeley RISC), and John Hennessy (Stanford MIPS) proved a revolutionary principle: complex microcode slows down the clock for everything, and the compiler can sequence simple instructions better than silicon.

Look at how 99% of developers run AI coding agents today:

  • They stuff 12 skills, a 2,000-line .cursorrules file, an MCP tool catalog, and 150,000 tokens of history into a single monolithic CISC context window, hoping the neural network will simultaneously simulate a project manager, a state machine, a code generator, a linter, and an adversarial code reviewer in one continuous stream.
  • Forcing an O(N^2) attention matrix on a $40,000 TPU to simulate a for loop and a Makefile is the 2026 equivalent of VAX microcode!

In our RISC Agentic Pipeline (SCAR-PROC-95):

  • The Harness Compiler (WORKFLOW.mk + POSIX state files) handles 100% of the deterministic sequencing, state persistence, SHA-256 Merkle tree locking, and risk-tier routing at zero token cost.
  • The TPU / LLM is used strictly for what it is best at: a single-cycle, fixed-width (15k–25k token) Cosine-Similarity ALU (Free Flow Between the Riverbanks). Each fork() subagent (Target 15 Archaeologist, Target 30 Red-Test Builder, Target 40 Six-Pillar Critic) wakes up in a clean context window provisioned only with the phase-bound scars S_Worker(T_k) for that exact target, does its one creative synthesis pass, writes its verified receipt to disk, and executes exit 0.

2. Why a One-Shot Prompt Could Never Have Invented This Workflow

Could you have walked up to Gemini, Claude, or ChatGPT two months ago and typed: "Write me the ultimate fault-tolerant software engineering workflow"?

No! Why? If all of Stuart Feldman's 1976 make, Antonio Damasio's 1994 neuroscience, Fernando Flores's 1986 speech-act theory, E.F. Codd's 1970 relational algebra, and Alan Kay's 1980 Smalltalk-80 were already sitting inside the model's pre-training weights, why didn't a one-shot prompt connect them?

flowchart TD
    C1["🌍 Continent 1: AI Prompt Checklists\n• 'You are a 10x engineer'\n• 'CRITICAL: DO NOT...'\n• Numbered prose checklists\n(Cosine distance ≈ 0 to 'AI workflow' query)"]
    C2["🏛️ Continent 2: 1970s–1980s Systems CS\n• Feldman (1976) GNU Make DAGs\n• Dijkstra (1975) Guarded Commands\n• Codd (1970) 3NF & Foreign Keys\n• Kay & Ingalls (1980) Smalltalk-80"]
    C3["🧠 Continent 3: Cognitive & Speech Science\n• Damasio (1994) Somatic Markers\n• Grinder & Bandler (1975) NLP Meta-Model\n• Flores (1986) Conversation for Action\n• Baron-Cohen (1985) Sally-Anne ToM"]

    Bridge["⚡ 60 Days of Socratic 'What If...' Bridges\n('What if compaction is a warm reboot and <brain>/state/ is /etc/init.d?')"]
    C1 -. "High-Voltage Cross-Domain Cables" .-> Bridge
    C2 --> Bridge
    C3 --> Bridge

In the pre-training corpus, those domains live on three disconnected continents separated by huge cosine-distance oceans! 3. The Unrecognized AGI Theorem (180 IQ Without Nociception) & Software as the Drosophila of All AGI

Once those cables are laid, a startling insight emerges: we already reached the neocortical threshold of AGI on all the major frontier models over the past year—nobody sees it yet because intelligence also requires scars to be complete. I came into this project just because I hated reading long diffs, and walked out recognizing that we already invented AGI; it just needed a nudge.

Imagine a human being with a 180 IQ, fluency in 100 languages, and encyclopedic knowledge of science, law, medicine, and engineering—but born with Congenital Insensitivity to Pain (CIP) and no amygdala. On a 5-minute multiple-choice exam (MMLU, SWE-bench), they score 99.9%. Put them in a commercial kitchen for four hours without supervision, and they lean their elbow on a 500°F stove burner, chase a shiny object out the window, and burn the restaurant down. (There should be a new name for experts: people who have avoided the second burn.)

If you misdiagnose missing pain receptors as missing intelligence, you will spend $100 billion trying to breed a 220-IQ chef—who will still lean their elbow on the stove burner!

5. Convergent Evolution & The 1988 "NO PERL PLEASE!" Playbook: Nine Practitioners Discovering the Same Physics

I watched sysadmins struggle to glue sed, awk, tr, cut, sort, and uniq into brittle 40-line shell pipelines that broke the moment a filename had a space or a newline in it. Whenever someone posted a gnarly problem—even when they started adding "NO PERL PLEASE!" to the subject line—I would give them a working 25-line Bourne shell pipeline, followed by:

"And by the way, here is the 2-line Perl script that does the exact same thing in 1/10th the time and won't break on spaces or newlines."

This brings us to the million-dollar question for frontier AI labs (Google DeepMind, Anthropic, OpenAI) and open-source model builders:

"Imagine that, with all the frontier models having been trained on 10 trillion happy paths, to finally start digging and differentiating the 100 billion sad paths, and burning those in as negative infinities. Even at peak data consumption, we can still separate the wheat from the chaff, to produce only wheat in the future."

Wait—if the 4 toxic tutorials on Page 1 of Google are sitting inside the model's pre-training weights right now, could frontier labs (or anyone with a single GPU and a LoRA) bake our -∞ scars directly into future model weights so a casual 1-line prompt "just does the right thing" on Turn 1?

Why the Frontier Labs Missed This: Goodhart's Law on SWE-bench

Why haven't frontier labs already burned sad-path scars into their post-training pipelines? Look at what they optimize for: SWE-bench Verified.

How does SWE-bench work? It spins up a temporary Docker container, lets the model edit a file to make a unit test pass, scores it 1.0, and immediately runs rm -rf on the container 10 seconds later!

  • Because there is no Day 2 in SWE-bench, a patch that leaks file descriptors, forgets cancel() on a stream, drops a database index, or swallows an async exception gets the exact same 100% leaderboard score as a battle-hardened production patch.
  • When your benchmark deletes the universe 10 seconds after the test turns green, sad paths carry zero evolutionary penalty.

articles.body_html:
Coding agents write frontend code fast, but they can't see it run. This is the flow I use to fix that, with a signup form that fails on submit as the example.

The Old Way

  1. The agent changes the form.
  2. You open the page, click submit, and nothing happens.
  3. You open DevTools, find a 422 in the Network tab, and copy the response.
  4. You paste it into the chat. The agent guesses a fix.
  5. You reload. Now the console shows a TypeError. You copy and paste again.

You're the agent's eyes, and most of your time goes to copying, not thinking.

The New Way

  1. You ask: "Submit the signup form on localhost:3000 and tell me why it fails."
  2. The agent clicks submit, reads the 422 response and the console, and matches them to the code.
  3. It explains the cause and proposes a fix.
  4. You check that explanation against what you see in the browser, then approve or push back. 
flowchart TB
  accTitle: The old way and the new way
  accDescr: In the old way, the agent writes code, the browser shows an error, and you copy that error back to the agent. In the new way, the agent reads the browser through MCP and reports its findings to you, and you validate them before it continues.
  subgraph Old
    direction TB
    a1[Agent] -- writes code --> b1[Browser]
    b1 -- error --> y1[You]
    y1 -- paste --> a1
  end
  subgraph New
    direction TB
    a2[Agent] -- writes code --> b2[Browser]
    b2 -- MCP --> a2
    a2 -- findings --> y2[You]
    y2 -- validate --> a2
  end
  Old ~~~ New

The copy-paste is gone. You're still there, in a different role.

This is human in the loop (HITL): the agent gathers evidence, and you validate it. Don't trust it 100%. It can misread a trace, or silence an error instead of fixing it.

The HITL notes in this post mark where to look yourself.

Cover Every Scenario

Browser access lets the agent put a page through every scenario your customers hit, not only the one where everything works:

Scenario What the customer should get
Success The flow works end to end
Slow A loading state, no double submits
Error A clear message, their input kept, a retry
Performance Fast loading, no layout shifts
Accessibility Works with a keyboard and a screen reader

The rest of this post shows how to set it up, then walks through each one.

The Tools

Two MCP servers give an agent a browser. MCP is an open standard, so neither is tied to Claude Code. Both work in Cursor, VS Code with Copilot, Codex, and Gemini CLI.

Chrome DevTools MCP

Chrome DevTools MCP is Google's MCP server for Chrome. It lets the agent open pages, click, and read what you see in DevTools:

  • Console: errors, warnings, and logs
  • Network: requests, status codes, and payloads
  • Performance: traces with Core Web Vitals like LCP and CLS
  • Accessibility: Lighthouse audits and the accessibility tree
  • Emulation: slow networks, offline mode, CPU throttling, dark mode, reduced motion, and forced colors

Playwright MCP

Playwright MCP is Microsoft's MCP server for browser automation. It drives Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, can make a single request fail, and helps the agent write end-to-end tests you can rerun.

Installing Them

Most agents read the same config:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "chrome-devtools": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
    },
    "playwright": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["@playwright/mcp@latest", "--caps=network"]
    }
  }
}

The --caps=network flag turns on Playwright MCP's request mocking. In Cursor, add the config under Settings > MCP. In VS Code, both READMEs have one-click install buttons.

In Claude Code, two commands add both:

claude mcp add chrome-devtools --scope user npx chrome-devtools-mcp@latest
claude mcp add playwright -- npx @playwright/mcp@latest --caps=network

Run /mcp to confirm they're connected. Then ask the agent to open your local app and list the console messages.

By default, Chrome DevTools MCP starts its own Chrome. To use the one you already have open, add --autoConnect. It needs Chrome 144 or later, with remote debugging allowed at chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging.

Which One When

Use both, for different jobs. Chrome DevTools MCP looks inside one page: debugging, comparing, and measuring. Playwright MCP fails requests on purpose and writes tests you can rerun in any browser.

flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a browser MCP server
  accDescr: To debug, compare pages, or measure performance in Chrome, use Chrome DevTools MCP. To write end-to-end tests, mock failed requests, or check Firefox and Safari, use Playwright MCP.
  need{What do you need?}
  need -- "debug, compare,<br>measure" --> devtools[Chrome DevTools MCP]
  need -- "e2e tests, mocks,<br>other browsers" --> playwright[Playwright MCP]

The Debug Loop

Start with the success path: the flow working end to end. With browser access, getting there follows the same loop every time.

The agent changes the code, reloads the page, and reads the signals. You review what it found and steer it when it chases the wrong cause.

flowchart TD
  accTitle: The debug loop
  accDescr: The agent edits the code, reloads the page, and reads the console, network, and performance trace. You review what it found. If the issue isn't fixed, you steer the agent and it edits again. When it's fixed, you ship.
  edit[Agent edits code] --> reload[Reload page] --> read[Agent reads signals]
  read --> review[You review findings]
  review --> fixed{Fixed?}
  fixed -- no, you steer --> edit
  fixed -- yes --> ship[Ship]

HITL: Keep the browser window visible while the agent works. When it says the bug is fixed, reproduce it yourself before you believe it.

The two signals you'll read most are console errors and network requests.

Console Errors

My prompt: "Open /signup, submit the form, and list the console errors. Explain the cause before changing anything."

The agent reads the error and its stack trace, opens the file it points to, and tells you what it thinks went wrong. You read that explanation before any code changes.

HITL: An error that disappears isn't always fixed. Check the diff: the agent may have wrapped it in a try/catch or removed the code that logged it.

Network Requests

My prompt: "Submit the form and show me the request and response for /api/signup. Compare the payload with what the backend expects."

The agent lists the requests, opens the failing one, and compares its body with the code that builds it. A misnamed field or a missing header shows up right there.

HITL: Check the request against the API spec, not the agent's reading of it. Changing the frontend to accept a broken response hides a backend bug.

Testing Slow and Failing Requests

Customers rarely see a crash. They see a failure handled badly: a spinner that never stops, a blank page, a form that loses what they typed. The agent can slow things down or break them on purpose and show you what customers see.

Each server does this differently:

  • Playwright MCP fails one request: browser_route makes an endpoint return a 500, a 404, or a malformed body.
  • Chrome DevTools MCP degrades the whole page: emulate sets Slow 3G, offline mode, or CPU throttling. It can't mock a single request.

My prompt, combining both: "Make POST /api/signup return a 500, submit the form, and screenshot what the user sees. Then try it on Slow 3G."

Slow

On Slow 3G or with the CPU throttled, check what the customer gets:

  • A loading state that shows up right away and ends, with an error if it takes too long
  • A submit button they can't press twice
  • Content that doesn't jump around when it arrives

Error

With a request failing, check what the customer gets:

  • A message in plain words that says what to do next, not a stack trace or raw JSON
  • Their input still in the form
  • A retry that works
  • Focus moved to the error, and the error announced to screen readers

Once a state looks right, lock it in with Playwright's page.route() so it stays that way:

test('signup keeps the input and offers a retry when the API fails', async ({
  page,
}) => {
  await page.route('**/api/signup', (route) => route.fulfill({ status: 500 }));
  await page.goto('/signup');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('ada@example.com');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign up' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Try again');
  await expect(page.getByLabel('Email')).toHaveValue('ada@example.com');
});

HITL: The agent can confirm an error message appears. Only you can judge whether it helps. Read each error state as a customer would: is it clear, kind, and does it say what to do next?

Improving Core Web Vitals

Slow requests are one side of speed. The other is how fast the page loads and settles, and that's where browser access helps most.

Without it, the agent guesses from the code. With it, the agent records a trace, sees which element is the LCP and what shifts the layout, and measures again after each change.

My prompt: "Record a performance trace of the home page with the CPU throttled 4x. Tell me the LCP element and what shifts the layout, then suggest one change at a time."

That turns "this might be faster" into numbers. The agent proposes a change, reruns the trace, and keeps it only if LCP or CLS improves.

HITL: Read the trace yourself before accepting a change. One run is noise, so ask for several. And the trade-offs are yours: preloading an image or inlining CSS can win a metric and cost something else.

Checking Accessibility

An accessible page works for every customer: people on a keyboard, on a screen reader, or who need more contrast or less motion. The agent can check part of this in the browser.

Chrome DevTools MCP runs a Lighthouse audit and reads the accessibility tree, the names and roles a screen reader announces. It also turns on the settings some customers rely on: forced colors, higher contrast, and reduced motion.

My prompt: "Run a Lighthouse accessibility audit on /signup, then tab through the form and tell me where the focus goes."

Lock the fixes in with axe in your Playwright tests:

import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';

test('signup has no detectable accessibility violations', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/signup');
  const results = await new AxeBuilder({ page }).analyze();
  expect(results.violations).toEqual([]);
});

HITL: Automated checks catch only some accessibility issues. A clean audit doesn't mean the page works with a screen reader. Tab through it yourself, and try VoiceOver or NVDA on the flows that matter.

Migrating Legacy Code Without Regressions

A migration has to keep every scenario working. The worst migration bug is a new page that looks almost like the old one, so capture how the legacy page behaves before you change anything.

Start with a Contract

Write down what must stay the same. This is the contract, and every test after it checks against it.

## Contract: /checkout

- Same visible text and layout at 390px and 1280px
- Same API requests, in the same order, with the same payloads
- No new console errors or warnings
- LCP and CLS no worse than the legacy page
- Every action reachable with the keyboard

The idea is the same as in MigFlow: agents need a contract, not a tutorial.

HITL: You write or approve the contract. The agent can draft it from the legacy page, but it can't know which behavior your users depend on.

Cover the Legacy Page with Tests

Many legacy projects have no end-to-end tests. With Playwright MCP, the agent walks through the legacy page in a real browser and writes a Playwright test for each line of the contract.

Run them against the legacy page first. They must pass there, so they describe what the page does today, quirks included.

Playwright's toHaveScreenshot() saves screenshots of the legacy page as the baseline. Visual changes then show up as a pixel diff, not a judgment call:

test('checkout looks the same as the legacy page', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('checkout.png', { fullPage: true });
});

Create the baseline from the legacy page with npx playwright test --update-snapshots. After that, every run compares against it.

HITL: Read every test. A test that passes no matter what protects nothing. Some quirks it captures are bugs you'll want to fix, not keep.

Migrate and Rerun the Same Tests

Now migrate, and run the same tests against the new page. A failing test is a regression. When one fails, the agent uses Chrome DevTools MCP to compare both pages and find out why.

The tests stay in CI after the migration, so the next change is covered too.

flowchart TD
  accTitle: Migrating without regressions
  accDescr: Write the contract, then cover the legacy page with Playwright tests. Migrate the code and run the same tests. If they fail, debug with Chrome DevTools MCP and migrate again. When they pass, you review and ship.
  contract[Write the contract] --> cover[Test the legacy page]
  cover --> migrate[Migrate the code]
  migrate --> pass{Same tests pass?}
  pass -- no --> debug[Debug with DevTools MCP]
  debug --> migrate
  pass -- yes --> review[You review and ship]

HITL: When a test fails, you decide whether the page or the test is wrong. Don't let the agent update a screenshot baseline or loosen an assertion to go green without your OK.

Limits

  • The agent can be confidently wrong. It will explain a wrong cause as clearly as a right one.
  • It's slower than reading the code when the bug is obvious.
  • Traces and logs fill the context window, so ask for the specific signal you need.
  • The agent can read cookies and local storage. Add --isolated for a temporary profile, and be careful with --autoConnect, which uses the Chrome you're signed in to.
  • Performance traces may send page URLs to Google's CrUX API. Add --no-performance-crux when you debug internal URLs.

Try It

Start with one prompt in any agent: "Open localhost:3000, list the console errors, and explain the cause before fixing anything."

Then try the other scenarios on one page: "Load the checkout page on Slow 3G, then with the payment request failing, and screenshot what the customer sees in each case."

Migrating a page? Write the contract, then ask: "Write Playwright tests for this contract and run them against the legacy page." Run the same tests after the migration.

A Tool in the Engineer's Hands

Success, slow, error, performance, accessibility: the agent can now put a page through every scenario and bring you the evidence. That's a powerful tool in the engineer's hands.

It doesn't decide what the evidence means. Every HITL note above comes down to the same habit: keep your eyes on the browser, and treat the agent's conclusions as claims to check, not facts.

As I wrote in AI Writes Code. You Own Quality., speed without judgment means shipping bugs faster. Browser access doesn't change who owns the fix. It gives you better evidence to own it with.

The agent gets eyes on the browser. You keep the judgment.

articles.title: AI Is Writing More Code Than Ever. But Are We Becoming Better Developers?
articles.description: AI can write code in seconds.  It can build a React component, create an API, fix bugs, generate...
articles.body_html:
AI can write code in seconds.

It can build a React component, create an API, fix bugs, generate database queries, write tests, and even work across an entire codebase without requiring a developer to touch every file.

A few years ago, these tasks could take hours or even days.

Today, an AI coding agent can complete a surprising amount of that work with a simple instruction.

But there is a question we should be asking:

If AI is making it easier to write software, are we actually becoming better software developers?

Or are we simply becoming better at asking machines to write code for us?

This is one of the biggest questions facing the software development industry in 2026.

1. AI Has Fundamentally Changed How We Write Code

Let's be honest. Software development is changing faster than many of us expected.

Tools such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, and other AI-powered coding assistants have changed the traditional development workflow.

Previously, developers generally followed a familiar process:

  • Understand the requirements.
  • Research the solution.
  • Write the code.
  • Debug errors.
  • Write tests.
  • Review and improve the implementation.
  • Deploy the application.

Now, a developer can describe a feature in natural language and ask an AI agent to handle several of these steps.

For example, instead of manually creating an authentication system, a developer might ask:

"Build a complete authentication system with email verification, password reset, secure sessions, and database integration. Follow the existing project architecture."

An AI coding agent can inspect the repository, create files, modify existing code, and propose an implementation.

The developer's role is increasingly shifting from writing every line to directing, reviewing, and validating the work.

This is not a small improvement to the development process.

It is a fundamental change in how software gets built.

2. The Numbers Show How Quickly AI Coding Is Growing

This transformation is not just based on personal observations.

GitHub's 2026 Octoverse report, published on October 28, provides some interesting numbers.

According to the report:

  • Developers pushed 17.9 billion times to GitHub over the reporting year.
  • GitHub recorded 34.3 billion commits across public and private repositories.
  • More than 1.3 billion pull requests were merged.
  • In September 2026, more than 40% of pull requests started with an AI agent, compared with 17% in March.

Think about that last number.

In just six months, the share of pull requests started by AI agents more than doubled.

AI is no longer simply suggesting the next line of code. It is increasingly participating in real software development workflows.

Developers are delegating tasks, reviewing generated implementations, and managing multiple AI-assisted workflows.

The industry is moving from AI-assisted coding toward AI-assisted software engineering.

Source: GitHub Octoverse 2026 coverage

3. The Biggest Risk: Developers May Stop Understanding Their Own Code

Here is where things become interesting.

AI can generate code quickly, but generating code and understanding code are two very different things.

Imagine a junior developer building an application with an AI coding agent.

The agent creates:

  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Database models and migrations.
  • API endpoints.
  • Frontend components.
  • Payment integration.
  • Error handling.
  • Automated tests.

The application works during initial testing.

The developer feels productive.

But what happens when something breaks in production?

What happens when two database operations create a race condition?

What happens when an API exposes sensitive information?

What happens when a subscription is charged twice?

What happens when a seemingly harmless change breaks another part of the application?

If the developer cannot understand the generated implementation, they may struggle to identify the actual problem.

This is the difference between producing software and engineering software.

AI can help you build something. It cannot automatically make you responsible for understanding what you have built.

That responsibility still belongs to the developer.

4. Writing Less Code Does Not Mean Understanding Less

I don't believe developers need to stop using AI to become better engineers.

In fact, avoiding AI completely could become a disadvantage.

The important thing is how we use it.

Consider two different approaches.

Developer A:

  • Gives AI a large task.
  • Accepts all generated changes.
  • Runs the application once.
  • Assumes everything is correct.
  • Moves to the next feature.

Developer B:

  • Understands the requirements before using AI.
  • Provides the correct architectural context.
  • Reviews the generated implementation.
  • Checks database changes and API behavior.
  • Tests edge cases.
  • Examines security implications.
  • Understands the final code before merging it.

Both developers use AI.

Both may produce features quickly.

But their engineering skills are developing in very different directions.

Developer A is becoming dependent on generated output.

Developer B is using AI to increase productivity while continuing to develop technical judgment.

That distinction will matter more as AI agents become capable of handling larger tasks.

5. Debugging Is Still One of the Most Important Developer Skills

There is something interesting about software development.

Writing the first version of a feature is often easier than maintaining it.

A feature might work perfectly with normal input but fail under unexpected conditions.

For example:

  • A user submits the same payment request twice.
  • Two users update the same database record simultaneously.
  • A network request times out after the server has already processed it.
  • An authentication token expires during an important operation.
  • A database migration works locally but fails in production.
  • A background job processes the same task multiple times.

These are not necessarily problems that can be solved by generating more code.

They require understanding how systems behave.

Developers need to understand:

  • Data flow.
  • Database transactions.
  • Concurrency.
  • API contracts.
  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Logging and monitoring.
  • Error handling.
  • System architecture.

AI can help investigate these problems, but developers must still evaluate whether the proposed solution is correct.

In an AI-driven development environment, debugging may become even more valuable because more generated code means more implementations that need careful verification.

6. The Junior Developer Problem Is Real

One concern I hear frequently is:

"If AI can write code, how will junior developers gain experience?"

Traditionally, junior developers learned through smaller tasks.

They fixed bugs, implemented simple components, wrote basic queries, and gradually learned how larger systems worked.

These tasks helped them understand the foundations of software engineering.

But if AI handles every small task, developers may miss opportunities to build those foundations.

A junior developer who asks AI to explain a database query and then studies the execution is learning.

A junior developer who copies the generated query without understanding it is missing an important opportunity.

The solution is not to ban AI from junior developers.

Instead, companies and senior engineers should encourage them to:

  1. Attempt small problems independently before asking AI.
  2. Ask AI to explain why a solution works.
  3. Review generated code line by line.
  4. Learn debugging instead of immediately requesting a complete rewrite.
  5. Understand the architecture behind the features they build.
  6. Practice solving problems without AI occasionally.

The goal should be to create developers who can work with AI, not developers who cannot work without it.

7. What Skills Will Matter Most for Developers in 2027?

The definition of a strong developer is changing.

Knowing programming syntax will remain useful, but it will not be enough.

I believe these skills will become increasingly important.

1. System Design

Understanding how frontend applications, backend services, databases, APIs, and infrastructure work together.

2. Code Review

Being able to identify incorrect assumptions, unnecessary complexity, security problems, and performance issues in AI-generated code.

3. Debugging

Understanding why something fails instead of repeatedly asking AI to generate another solution.

4. Security

Knowing how authentication, authorization, data validation, encryption, and secure API design work.

5. AI Agent Management

Learning how to break large tasks into smaller steps, provide context, manage agent workflows, and verify results.

6. Product Thinking

Understanding what users actually need, why a feature matters, and whether the implementation solves the real problem.

7. Independent Problem-Solving

Being able to reason about a technical problem without depending entirely on an AI-generated answer.

These skills complement AI rather than compete with it.

8. AI Should Make Developers More Capable, Not More Dependent

I use a simple principle when thinking about AI-assisted development:

Never merge code that you cannot explain.

You do not necessarily need to type every line yourself.

You do not need to memorize every framework function.

You do not need to manually create every component or database migration.

But you should understand the important decisions behind the implementation.

If an AI agent changes your database schema, understand the migration.

If it modifies authentication, understand the security implications.

If it creates an API, understand the request, response, validation, and error-handling behavior.

If it builds a feature, understand how that feature interacts with the rest of your application.

Use AI to remove repetitive work, accelerate research, explore alternative implementations, and improve your workflow.

But do not outsource your engineering judgment.

That is the skill that makes you a developer rather than simply an operator of coding tools.

9. My Prediction: The Best Developers Will Become AI-Orchestrated Engineers

I don't think AI will simply eliminate the need for software developers.

I think it will change what makes someone a valuable developer.

In the past, productivity was often associated with how efficiently someone could write, debug, and deliver code.

In the coming years, productivity will increasingly involve how effectively someone can:

  • Understand a complex problem.
  • Design a reliable solution.
  • Delegate suitable tasks to AI agents.
  • Coordinate multiple development workflows.
  • Review and validate generated implementations.
  • Maintain systems over time.
  • Take responsibility for the final product.

One developer with strong engineering fundamentals and effective AI workflows may be able to accomplish work that previously required a much larger team.

But that does not mean engineering knowledge becomes less important.

It may become more important.

When AI can generate hundreds of lines of code in minutes, knowing whether those lines should exist in the first place becomes a valuable skill.

Final Thoughts

AI is making software development more accessible, faster, and increasingly powerful.

That is a good thing.

More people can experiment with ideas, build applications, automate workflows, and solve problems that previously required extensive technical knowledge.

But we should not confuse faster code generation with better engineering.

A developer who understands the system, questions assumptions, reviews implementations, and takes responsibility for the final result will always have an advantage over someone who blindly accepts generated code.

We are entering an era where writing code may become less of a bottleneck.

Understanding, designing, reviewing, and maintaining software will matter even more.

The question is no longer just how much code you can write. It is how well you understand the software you create.

And perhaps that is what will separate great developers from everyone else in the AI era.

What Do You Think?

I would love to hear other developers' experiences.

  1. Are AI coding agents making you a better developer, or are you becoming more dependent on them?
  2. Should junior developers learn programming fundamentals before using AI coding tools?
  3. Will system design, debugging, and code review become more valuable than writing code?

Share your thoughts in the comments. I am especially interested in hearing from developers who are already using AI agents in real production projects.

articles.title: TEAM Portability: Six Months of Rebuilding How I Work with AI
articles.description: I thought AI retraining would mostly mean learning to produce software faster: pick the right model,...
articles.body_html:
I thought AI retraining would mostly mean learning to produce software faster: pick the right model, wire up agents, and let throughput carry the rest.

Six months later, I've rebuilt how I work with AI across Codenames AI (an online word game), automated writing workflows, dependency management, and the tools supporting them. Along the way, I've published weekly field reports on DEV.to documenting what broke and what I learned.

The bigger change was not typing speed. It was how I decide what software should do, how I verify it, where I place trust before I merge or ship, and how I carry those habits from one codebase to the next. Looking back across those field reports, I started seeing the same questions recur. Those questions eventually became four recurring disciplines: Taste, Evals & Verification, Authority, and Measurement. Portability became the fifth: making those practices work consistently across projects, tools, and agents. Together, I think of them as TEAM Portability. I did not design that map upfront; it emerged from what kept breaking once the tooling started working.

Taste

Reloading a Codenames AI tab restored the board while leftover targeting highlights lit up cards I had never clicked on the new board. The persisted game state was truthful; the drafting UI was lying about what I had targeted. I found that while exercising mode switches locally, but green CI had nothing to say about the mismatch.

The problem went beyond clearing stale highlights. I had to decide which parts of a player's work should survive a reload and which were temporary drafting intent. I ran into a similar gap when a resume generator passed every pipeline check but still produced something I wouldn't submit.

Both experiences showed me that correct implementation isn't enough when the product requirements are incomplete. Tests can verify the behavior we've specified, but I still need to decide whether that behavior makes sense for the person using the product.

Evals & Verification

While building my writing workflow, I discovered that one strong published example communicated my expectations better than an expanding collection of writing rules. It was easier to show the AI what good writing looked like than to describe every decision behind it.

Evaluating that writing presented a different challenge. My AI reviewer gave a draft 23/25 while missing important editorial problems. I changed the reviewer to analyze drafts before scoring them, so the assessment followed an editorial read rather than driving it.

Even that wasn't enough. As I continued refining the reviewer, I found that separating different kinds of reasoning worked better than expanding the rubric. Challenging an initial assessment, identifying redundant prose, and checking whether a section served the reader each needed deliberate attention.

Together, these experiences changed how I approach evaluation. Clear expectations matter, but so does the process used to assess whether they're met. I still need to decide what quality looks like for a particular task and whether the checks can recognize it.

Authority

While building Savepoints, I expected the agent host to provide reliable lifecycle signals for deciding when completed work needed review. The host didn't. Events were available, but I couldn't safely infer everything I needed about which work had finished or which repository it affected.

Other projects exposed different kinds of missing boundaries. A multi-step agent plan listed every step except where to stop, and an agent merged a PR I expected to review. Separately, Git reported success while hooks never ran in a worktree that lacked the required executable shims.

These weren't identical failures, but they challenged the same assumption: that a boundary existed because I'd described or configured it. I now make execution authority explicit, establish which host signals I can rely on, and check that safeguards actually operate in the environment doing the work.

Measurement

On Codenames AI, the Active players tile looked convincing until I asked which sessions belonged in the number. The dashboard was counting events correctly, but it couldn't distinguish production players from activity on preview deployments. I was reading the number as evidence of real players without knowing which environments contributed to it.

Other experiments exposed different ways that apparently useful signals could mislead me. A production model swap surfaced contract and validation gaps, making it difficult to separate model performance from weaknesses in the surrounding application. And when a Sankey chart of my job applications disagreed with the underlying records, I had to distinguish problems in the data from problems in how it was transformed and displayed.

The common lesson wasn't that the numbers were wrong. It was that interpreting them required understanding what they represented, how they were produced, and which assumptions sat between the underlying events and the result I was looking at.

Portability

I first tried to solve portability by copying one repo's agent setup into the next. That worked until assumptions tied to each product and shared workflows started drifting apart. I eventually separated reusable policy and procedures from the tools and mechanics that belonged to each repository.

That solved how to share the methodology, but not how to keep individual repositories aligned with it. Plans still drifted until structure became checkable in CI. The validator couldn't judge whether a plan was good, but it could verify that the required structure was present.

Working with a remote cloud agent exposed another boundary. Briefing it felt like onboarding a new hire because it didn't automatically inherit my local reasoning or authenticated tools. That separation required a more deliberate handoff, but also made independent execution possible.

Portability, I've learned, isn't copying the same configuration everywhere. It's carrying the same engineering expectations into different environments while accounting for what each environment needs to establish independently.

Six months in, with more to build

Over the past six months, I've experimented with AI across different projects and kept running into the same questions: what outcome matters, what evidence proves it, where the agent must stop, what the numbers actually count, and whether those practices survive in the next codebase.

There's still plenty I want to build and learn, but I'm heading overseas for a few weeks. Six months felt like a good point to reflect on what I've learned so far. When I return, I'll have TEAM Portability as a framework to approach new problems, test what I've learned, and refine my practices as I go.

Takeaway: Getting better at AI-assisted engineering isn't just about learning new tools or producing software faster. It's about developing the judgment to define good outcomes, verify results, set boundaries, understand measurements, and carry those practices into new environments.

articles.title: My Struct Key Boxed Itself Two Million Times
articles.description: A dictionary lookup shouldn't allocate, so why was mine showing up in the profiler? The culprit was a struct key missing one interface, boxing itself on every call.
articles.body_html:
I had a cache keyed on a little struct. Three ints bundled together, nothing to it, the kind of value type you reach for when a plain tuple feels too anonymous. Over a batch of work I'd look things up in a Dictionary keyed by that struct a couple million times, and one day that lookup loop showed up in an allocation profile. Which made no sense to me. A dictionary lookup doesn't allocate. It hashes a key, walks a bucket, compares. Where's the garbage coming from?

The garbage was the key. Every lookup was boxing it, and I'd never typed a new to make that happen.

Who compares your keys

When you put something in a Dictionary<TKey, TValue>, the dictionary needs two things from the key: a hash code, and a way to tell two keys apart. It gets both from EqualityComparer<TKey>.Default, and which comparer that resolves to depends on your type. I'd never once thought about it, so I had the sample print it:

PlainKey -> ObjectEqualityComparer`1
FastKey  -> GenericEqualityComparer`1

Two structs, same three int fields, landing on different comparers. The only thing separating them is that one implements IEquatable<T> and the other doesn't.

GenericEqualityComparer<T> is the one you want. It calls your IEquatable<T>.Equals(T) directly, taking the struct by value. No boxing, no reflection.

ObjectEqualityComparer<T> is the fallback for everything else, and it's where my struct landed. It only knows the two methods every object has: object.GetHashCode() and object.Equals(object). Both live on object, so to call them on a struct the runtime has to box it first. And since I'd never written those methods myself, the ones it ends up calling are ValueType's defaults, which work out your fields by reflection at runtime. So every lookup boxed my key to hash it, then boxed it again to compare it.

The bill

Here's what that cost, next to the same struct with the methods filled in. Two million lookups into a two-hundred-thousand-entry dictionary, keys built up front so only the lookups land on the scorecard, best of five in a cloud container. I care about the ratio more than the millisecond:

PlainKey (default equality)      192,000,040 bytes    695.8 ms
FastKey (IEquatable<T>)                    40 bytes    236.5 ms

A hundred and ninety-two megabytes of boxes, for lookups that should allocate nothing at all. That works out to about ninety-six bytes of garbage per lookup, a few short-lived boxes each time, all of it piling into gen0 for the collector to deal with later. And close to three times slower on the clock, because reflection-based equality isn't cheap even before you count the allocations. The checksums matched, so both versions found the same entries and did the same work. One just made a mess doing it.

The fix is three methods, or one keyword

Spelling it out is mechanical:

struct FastKey(int x, int y, int z) : IEquatable<FastKey>
{
    public readonly int X = x, Y = y, Z = z;
    public bool Equals(FastKey other) => X == other.X && Y == other.Y && Z == other.Z;
    public override bool Equals(object? obj) => obj is FastKey o && Equals(o);
    public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(X, Y, Z);
}

The IEquatable<FastKey>.Equals is the line that moves you onto the fast comparer. The object.Equals override keeps the two agreeing with each other, which the analyzer nags you about anyway. And HashCode.Combine saves you from hand-rolling a hash that distributes badly.

Or skip all of it and let the compiler do the typing: record struct FastKey(int X, int Y, int Z) generates IEquatable<T>, both Equals methods, and a GetHashCode for you. That's what I reach for now. If a value type has any chance of becoming a dictionary key, a HashSet member, or the input to a LINQ Distinct or Contains, I make it a record struct from the start and stop thinking about it.

When it doesn't matter

If you never use the struct as a key and never compare two of them, none of this ever fires, and adding the methods is just noise for the next person reading the file. A struct that's pure data moving from here to there doesn't need an equality contract. The trap is the quiet upgrade: a value type that was perfectly fine as a plain bag of fields, right up until someone drops it into a dictionary and the boxing starts without a single compiler warning. Nothing tells you. The code builds, the lookups return the right answers, and the only evidence is a line in an allocation graph you weren't looking at.

One caveat on the fix itself. If you hand-write GetHashCode, keep it away from any field you plan to mutate while the struct is sitting in a hash-based collection. A key whose hash changes after it's stored is a different bug, and a nastier one to find. For keys I keep every field readonly, which the sample does.

Normally I'd link the runnable sample on GitHub, but the sandbox this ran in couldn't push to my samples repo this time, so here's the whole thing. Drop it in a net10.0 console project and dotnet run -c Release:

using System.Diagnostics;

const int Distinct = 200_000;
const int Lookups = 2_000_000;

var plainKeys = new PlainKey[Distinct];
var fastKeys = new FastKey[Distinct];
for (int i = 0; i < Distinct; i++)
{
    plainKeys[i] = new PlainKey(i, i * 3, i * 7);
    fastKeys[i] = new FastKey(i, i * 3, i * 7);
}

var plainMap = new Dictionary<PlainKey, long>(Distinct);
var fastMap = new Dictionary<FastKey, long>(Distinct);
for (int i = 0; i < Distinct; i++)
{
    plainMap[plainKeys[i]] = i;
    fastMap[fastKeys[i]] = i;
}

var rng = new Random(99);
int[] order = new int[Lookups];
for (int i = 0; i < Lookups; i++) order[i] = rng.Next(Distinct);

long LookupPlain()
{
    long hits = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < Lookups; i++)
        if (plainMap.TryGetValue(plainKeys[order[i]], out long v)) hits += v;
    return hits;
}

long LookupFast()
{
    long hits = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < Lookups; i++)
        if (fastMap.TryGetValue(fastKeys[order[i]], out long v)) hits += v;
    return hits;
}

(long bytes, double ms, long checksum) Measure(Func<long> run)
{
    long bestBytes = long.MaxValue;
    double bestMs = double.MaxValue;
    long checksum = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < 5; r++)
    {
        GC.Collect();
        GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
        GC.Collect();
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        checksum = run();
        sw.Stop();
        long bytes = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;
        if (bytes < bestBytes) bestBytes = bytes;
        if (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds < bestMs) bestMs = sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
    }
    return (bestBytes, bestMs, checksum);
}

Console.WriteLine("Comparer the runtime picks for each key:");
Console.WriteLine($"  PlainKey -> {EqualityComparer<PlainKey>.Default.GetType().Name}");
Console.WriteLine($"  FastKey  -> {EqualityComparer<FastKey>.Default.GetType().Name}");

_ = LookupPlain();
_ = LookupFast();

var plain = Measure(LookupPlain);
var fast = Measure(LookupFast);

Console.WriteLine($"{"PlainKey",-28}{plain.bytes,16:N0} bytes{plain.ms,10:F1} ms");
Console.WriteLine($"{"FastKey",-28}{fast.bytes,16:N0} bytes{fast.ms,10:F1} ms");
Console.WriteLine($"checksums: {plain.checksum} / {fast.checksum}");

struct PlainKey(int x, int y, int z)
{
    public readonly int X = x, Y = y, Z = z;
}

struct FastKey(int x, int y, int z) : IEquatable<FastKey>
{
    public readonly int X = x, Y = y, Z = z;
    public bool Equals(FastKey other) => X == other.X && Y == other.Y && Z == other.Z;
    public override bool Equals(object? obj) => obj is FastKey o && Equals(o);
    public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(X, Y, Z);
}

So, do you default your small value types to record struct, or only reach for equality once something starts leaking?
