articles.title: Five Agents in Split Panes: How xterm.js Draws Text With a WebGL Glyph Atlas
articles.description: Five coding agents streaming into five panes all share one main thread. How xterm.js draws text, DOM vs WebGL, and a benchmark you can run.
articles.body_html:
• Book: System Design Pocket Guide: Interviews
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You split the window five ways. Claude Code is printing a diff in one pane, Codex is running a test suite in another, and a third agent is dumping a 4,000-line build log because you asked it to "check why CI fails." Every one of those panes is a terminal emulator, and in an Electron or Tauri app, or in a browser tab, every one of them is JavaScript drawing characters into the same web page.

Nobody picks an agent setup by asking how the terminal paints glyphs. But when five streams arrive at once, the renderer decides whether the window stays responsive or whether your keystrokes land late. Here is how xterm.js, the terminal component inside VS Code, actually puts text on screen, and a small page you can use to measure it on your own machine.

A terminal is a grid with a 16.6 ms budget

A terminal emulator holds a grid of cells. Each cell has a character, a foreground color, a background color and style flags. Bytes from the process go through a parser that updates the grid, and a renderer turns the visible rows into pixels.

At 60 frames per second you get 16.6 ms per frame for everything on the page's main thread. That number is the budget the VS Code team used when they moved the terminal renderer from the DOM to canvas in 2017, and it still frames the problem.

xterm.js does not redraw on every write. Its RenderDebouncer asks for one requestAnimationFrame and, while that request is pending, widens the dirty range with Math.min on the start row and Math.max on the end row. A thousand writes inside one frame become one render of the rows they touched. Only rows in the viewport get drawn, never the scrollback.

So the renderer's cost is per frame, not per byte. The parser is the part that scales with output. Keep those two apart, because they behave differently when you add panes.

The DOM renderer: spans, layout, garbage

The renderer built into xterm.js core builds HTML. Since xterm.js 6.0 removed the canvas addon, it is that or WebGL. For each dirty row, DomRenderer calls replaceChildren with fresh nodes from DomRendererRowFactory. The factory is careful: it creates one <span> per run of adjacent cells that share background, foreground and style, rather than one per cell. Plain log lines collapse into a few spans per row.

Color-heavy output does not collapse. Agent output is full of ANSI color: green tool names, red diff lines, dim timestamps. Every color change starts a new span. After that the browser has to style, lay out and paint those nodes, and the old nodes become garbage.

The 2017 VS Code post put the ceiling plainly: with a DOM renderer, "performance will always have the hard cap imposed by the layout engine." It also says that composing and laying out the elements "could take longer than a frame (16.6ms) all by itself," and that under heavy output the old renderer dropped "below 10 FPS" (source). That post describes an older DOM renderer, but the shape of the cost is the same: more spans per frame, more layout per frame.


The atlas idea: draw each glyph once into a texture, then copy tiles out of it for every cell that needs that glyph.

The WebGL renderer: rasterise on first use, then copy quads

@xterm/addon-webgl replaces all of that with a WebGL2 renderer. The trick is the glyph atlas.

The first time a cell needs a glyph in a given style, TextureAtlas draws it with the 2D canvas API into a texture page and caches its coordinates. The cache key is the character plus its background, foreground and extended attributes, so a red x and a green x are two entries. Every later cell with that same key is a lookup, not a draw. Pages start at 512 px; when the atlas runs out of page slots, four same-sized pages are merged into one page twice as wide and twice as tall, as long as that stays under the texture-size limit (4096 px when no other limit is set). If they can't be merged, the atlas is evicted and starts over. During idle callbacks it also pre-fills printable ASCII so the first screen of output is mostly cache hits.

Then the drawing. GlyphRenderer keeps a typed array with 11 floats (44 bytes) per cell: offset, size, texture page, texture coordinates, texture size and cell position. Each of those attributes advances once per instance. The whole visible grid then goes to the GPU in a single call:

gl.drawElementsInstanced(
  gl.TRIANGLE_STRIP, 4, gl.UNSIGNED_BYTE, 0,
  bufferLength / Constants.INDICES_PER_CELL
);

That is one unit quad with four vertices, drawn once per cell. The CPU's job per frame shrinks to filling a float array for the dirty rows; there are no DOM nodes to lay out and no discarded spans to collect. The fragment shader picks the right texture page from an array of samplers, up to 32 pages or the device's texture-unit limit, whichever is lower.

One detail matters for split panes. In CharAtlasCache, terminals whose font and color configuration match share one atlas: the cache finds an entry with an equal config and adds the new terminal to its ownedBy list. Five panes with the same theme rasterise a glyph once, not five times.

What WebGL does not fix

The xterm.js flow control guide puts the terminal's input throughput at "5 - 35 MB/s", against producers that can push "several GB/s." Most of that is parsing, and the parser is the same code under both renderers. write() buffers and returns at once, and the buffer has a hard limit: "Any data beyond that limit gets discarded." Five agents flooding at once still share that parsing time on one main thread. WebGL frees up the frame budget the DOM renderer was spending on layout, and that time goes back to parsing and to your input.

WebGL can also go away under you. The addon's README warns that browsers "may drop WebGL contexts for various reasons like OOM or after the system has been suspended," and exposes onContextLoss so the app can dispose the addon. When an app does that, it ends up back on the DOM renderer. VS Code's default, per its terminal appearance docs, is auto: try WebGL, "fall back to the DOM renderer" if that fails. The same page lists Linux VMs, browsers without WebGL and outdated drivers as places where WebGL may not work well.

In code, the defensive load looks like this:

import { WebglAddon } from '@xterm/addon-webgl';

function loadWebgl(term) {
  try {
    const webgl = new WebglAddon();
    webgl.onContextLoss(() => webgl.dispose());
    term.loadAddon(webgl);
    return true;
  } catch {
    return false; // stays on the DOM renderer
  }
}

If you have ever seen one pane in a terminal app suddenly feel slower after the laptop woke from sleep, a dropped context and a silent fallback is one candidate worth checking.

A benchmark you can run

Save this as bench.html, serve the folder (npx serve . works), and open it twice: once with ?r=dom and once with ?r=webgl. It writes about 200,000 colored log lines in 200 chunks, waits for each chunk's write callback, and records how often the page managed to paint while it was busy.

<!doctype html>
<link rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://unpkg.com/@xterm/xterm@6.0.0/css/xterm.css">
<div id="t" style="width:900px;height:500px"></div>
<pre id="out"></pre>
<script type="module">
import { Terminal } from 'https://esm.sh/@xterm/xterm@6.0.0';
import { WebglAddon }
  from 'https://esm.sh/@xterm/addon-webgl@0.19.0';

const q = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
const mode = q.get('r') ?? 'dom';
const term = new Terminal({ scrollback: 1000 });
term.open(document.getElementById('t'));
if (mode === 'webgl') term.loadAddon(new WebglAddon());

const line = (i) =>
  `\x1b[32m[agent]\x1b[0m step ${i} src/f${i % 97}.ts ` +
  `\x1b[33mok\x1b[0m ${'.'.repeat(i % 40)}\r\n`;
const chunks = [];
for (let c = 0; c < 200; c++) {
  let s = '';
  for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) s += line(c * 1000 + i);
  chunks.push(s);
}

let frames = 0, worst = 0, last = performance.now();
let running = true;
const tick = (now) => {
  frames++;
  worst = Math.max(worst, now - last);
  last = now;
  if (running) requestAnimationFrame(tick);
};
requestAnimationFrame(tick);

const t0 = performance.now();
for (const chunk of chunks) {
  await new Promise((done) => term.write(chunk, done));
}
running = false;
const ms = performance.now() - t0;
document.getElementById('out').textContent =
  `${mode}: ${ms.toFixed(0)} ms, ${frames} frames, ` +
  `worst gap ${worst.toFixed(1)} ms`;
</script>

Read the three numbers together. Total time is mostly parser time, so expect it to move less than you'd guess. Frame count and worst gap are the renderer's story: how often the page got to paint, and the longest stretch where it couldn't. A long worst gap is the keystroke that shows up late. To mimic five panes, duplicate the div and the terminal five times and write to all of them in the same loop.

I haven't run this across a range of machines, so I won't quote numbers. Run it on yours, and on the oldest laptop you can borrow. The write callback fires when the parser finishes a chunk, per the write API docs, not when pixels hit the screen, so the final frame lands a moment after the total.

Where Hermes IDE sits in this

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes runs each agent (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI and others) in its own real terminal, with split panes so sessions sit side by side. Those terminals are xterm.js: the package.json pins @xterm/xterm 6.0.0 and depends on @xterm/addon-webgl. The README describes the rendering as "GPU-accelerated (WebGL) where the system supports it," which is the same try-WebGL, keep-DOM-as-fallback idea VS Code uses.


Hermes 2.3.4: Codex and Claude Code in split panes, each in its own hermes/ worktree, with the sessions sidebar showing status, context use, cost and branch.

None of that is specific to Hermes. Any app built on xterm.js can load the same addon, and VS Code has done so by default since its 1.55 release. Hermes is free to download, source-available under BSL 1.1, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and is not affiliated with any agent vendor. Download it here, or read the code on GitHub.

If this was useful

The glyph atlas is a small system-design lesson hiding in a terminal: a cache keyed on exactly what makes an entry unique, an eviction plan for when it fills, batching a thousand updates into one unit of work per frame, and sharing one expensive resource across tenants with the same config. Those are the trade-offs interviewers want you to say out loud. The System Design Pocket Guide: Interviews walks through 15 real designs step by step, with that reasoning on every page.

articles.title: The Tests Are Green. Did the Agent Follow the Spec?
articles.description: When a coding agent writes the feature and the tests, a green test suite only tells you that its code...
articles.body_html:
When a coding agent writes the feature and the tests, a green test suite only tells you that its code agrees with its tests. Neither of those is your spec.

I wrote a guide to spec-driven development that covers how to write a spec for an agent and how to work with one in Claude Code, Spec Kit, OpenSpec and Kiro. Near the end I say the agent can still ignore the spec, so you still need tests and a review. This post picks up from there, with two checks that run in CI:

  1. A small script that proves every acceptance criterion has a test that really ran and passed.
  2. Mutation testing, which proves those tests fail when the code is wrong.

Everything below comes from a real run with Node 24, Vitest 5.0.5 and Stryker 10.1.1. You can copy the code as it is.

The setup: a small spec and a weak implementation

The spec is a shorter version of the CSV export example from the guide. The only thing I added is a stable ID on each criterion, so that a machine can follow it:

# Spec: Export transactions to CSV

## Acceptance criteria
- AC-1: WHEN the user exports with no filters
  THEN all their transactions are included, newest first.
- AC-2: WHEN a description contains a comma or quotes
  THEN the field is quoted and escaped (RFC 4180).
- AC-3: WHEN the filtered list is empty
  THEN the file has only the header row.

If you use Spec Kit, you already have IDs: its template numbers requirements as FR-001. You'd only change one regex in the script.

Then I wrote the code badly on purpose. It has a real bug, because escapeField handles commas and forgets about quotes:

// src/csv.js
const COLUMNS = ['date', 'description', 'category', 'account', 'amount']

function escapeField(value) {
  const text = String(value)
  if (text.includes(',')) return `"${text}"`
  return text
}

export function buildCsv(rows) {
  const sorted = [...rows].sort((a, b) => b.date.localeCompare(a.date))
  const lines = sorted.map((row) =>
    COLUMNS.map((column) => escapeField(row[column])).join(','),
  )
  return [COLUMNS.join(','), ...lines].join('\n')
}

The tests are weak on purpose too. Each one names its criterion in the title, and one of them is skipped. In the demo they sit inside a describe('buildCsv', ...) block, which is where the buildCsv > prefix in the reports below comes from:

// src/csv.test.js
import { expect, it } from 'vitest'
import { buildCsv } from './csv.js'

const row = (over = {}) => ({
  date: '2026-10-01',
  description: 'Coffee',
  category: 'Food',
  account: 'Checking',
  amount: 4.5,
  ...over,
})

it('AC-1: includes all transactions', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([row(), row({ date: '2026-10-02' })])
  expect(csv.split('\n')).toHaveLength(3)
})

it('AC-2: escapes commas and quotes', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([row({ description: 'Coffee, "large"' })])
  expect(csv).toContain('Coffee')
})

it.skip('AC-3: empty list gives only the header', () => {
  expect(buildCsv([])).toBe('date,description,category,account,amount')
})

Vitest is happy with this:

Tests  2 passed | 1 skipped (3)

A grep for the IDs is happy as well, since all three appear in the test file.

Check 1: does each criterion have a test that ran and passed?

The usual way to link specs to tests is to search the test files for the IDs. That search can't see .skip, so it would miss AC-3 here. The test runner knows what happened, so I read its report.

Have Vitest write JUnit XML:

// vitest.config.js
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config'

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    reporters: ['default', 'junit'],
    outputFile: { junit: 'reports/junit.xml' },
  },
})

Then compare the report with the spec:

// scripts/check-spec.mjs
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'

const [specPath = 'SPEC.md', junitPath = 'reports/junit.xml'] =
  process.argv.slice(2)
const ID = /\bAC-\d+\b/g

const specIds = new Set(readFileSync(specPath, 'utf8').match(ID) ?? [])

// id -> list of test outcomes: 'passed', 'failed' or 'skipped'
const results = new Map()
const junit = readFileSync(junitPath, 'utf8')
const testcases = junit.matchAll(
  /<testcase\b([^>]*?)(\/>|>([\s\S]*?)<\/testcase>)/g,
)

for (const [, attrs, , body = ''] of testcases) {
  const name = attrs.match(/\bname="([^"]*)"/)?.[1] ?? ''
  const outcome = body.includes('<skipped')
    ? 'skipped'
    : /<(failure|error)\b/.test(body)
      ? 'failed'
      : 'passed'

  for (const id of name.match(ID) ?? []) {
    results.set(id, [...(results.get(id) ?? []), outcome])
  }
}

const problems = []

for (const id of specIds) {
  const outcomes = results.get(id) ?? []
  if (outcomes.length === 0) problems.push(`${id}: no test`)
  else if (outcomes.includes('failed')) problems.push(`${id}: failing`)
  else if (!outcomes.includes('passed')) problems.push(`${id}: only skipped tests`)
}

for (const id of results.keys()) {
  if (!specIds.has(id)) problems.push(`${id}: test exists, not in spec`)
}

if (problems.length > 0) {
  console.error(`Spec check failed:\n  ${problems.join('\n  ')}`)
  process.exit(1)
}

console.log(`Spec check passed: ${specIds.size} criteria covered.`)

Run it against the code above:

$ node scripts/check-spec.mjs
Spec check failed:
  AC-3: only skipped tests

The last loop runs in the other direction and catches drift. When I renamed AC-3 to AC-4 in the spec, leaving the tests alone, both sides were reported:

Spec check failed:
  AC-4: no test
  AC-3: test exists, not in spec

The same script also worked unchanged on the JUnit output of Node's built-in runner (node --test --test-reporter=junit). Jest and Playwright can write JUnit too, but I didn't test those, so check how they mark skipped tests.

I removed the .skip, and the script went green:

Tests  3 passed (3)
Spec check passed: 3 criteria covered.

The feature is still wrong, though. The code doesn't escape quotes, and nothing tests the sort order. This script can only tell you that a test exists and passes. It has no idea whether expect(csv).toContain('Coffee') proves anything.

Check 2: would the tests notice if the code were wrong?

Mutation testing changes your code in small ways (it flips a condition, removes a method call, empties a string) and runs the tests against each changed version, called a mutant. If the tests still pass, the mutant survived, and that line of code isn't really being tested.

This is the question to ask about tests written by an agent, and you don't have to read them all to get an answer. Install Stryker:

npm i -D @stryker-mutator/core @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner

Add a config:

{
  "testRunner": "vitest",
  "mutate": ["src/csv.js"],
  "reporters": ["clear-text", "progress"],
  "coverageAnalysis": "perTest"
}

Then npx stryker run. It took 3 seconds on this one file and found 6 survivors out of 21 mutants, for a score of 71.43%. These two are the interesting ones:

[Survived] ConditionalExpression
src/csv.js:5:7
-     if (text.includes(',')) return `"${text}"`
+     if (false) return `"${text}"`
Tests ran:
    buildCsv > AC-1: includes all transactions
    buildCsv > AC-2: escapes commas and quotes

[Survived] MethodExpression
src/csv.js:10:18
-     const sorted = [...rows].sort((a, b) => b.date.localeCompare(a.date))
+     const sorted = [...rows]
Tests ran:
    buildCsv > AC-1: includes all transactions
    buildCsv > AC-2: escapes commas and quotes
    buildCsv > AC-3: empty list gives only the header

The first mutant turns off the escaping entirely, and the AC-2 test still passes. The second deletes the sort, and the AC-1 test still passes. Those are the two features the spec asked for, and because the tests are named after criteria, the report points straight at the criteria with fake coverage.

Fixing what the mutants found

No mutant mentions the quotes bug. Stryker changes the code that exists, and the quote handling was never written. The mutant on line 5 only tells you the AC-2 test is too weak, and you find the bug when you fix the test:

const HEADER = 'date,description,category,account,amount'

it('AC-1: includes all transactions, newest first', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([
    row({ date: '2026-10-01' }),
    row({ date: '2026-10-03' }),
    row({ date: '2026-10-02' }),
  ])
  expect(csv.split('\n')).toEqual([
    HEADER,
    '2026-10-03,Coffee,Food,Checking,4.5',
    '2026-10-02,Coffee,Food,Checking,4.5',
    '2026-10-01,Coffee,Food,Checking,4.5',
  ])
})

it('AC-2: quotes fields with commas', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([row({ description: 'Coffee, large' })])
  expect(csv).toContain(',"Coffee, large",')
})

it('AC-2: escapes quotes by doubling them', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([row({ description: 'The "large" one' })])
  expect(csv).toContain(',"The ""large"" one",')
})

it('AC-3: empty list gives only the header', () => {
  expect(buildCsv([])).toBe(HEADER)
})

Now the bug shows up:

FAIL  src/csv.test.js > buildCsv > AC-2: escapes quotes by doubling them
Tests  1 failed | 3 passed (4)

Spec check failed:
  AC-2: failing

The fix is one line:

if (/[",]/.test(text)) return `"${text.replaceAll('"', '""')}"`

After that, the spec check passes and Stryker kills all 23 mutants, for a score of 100%. Don't expect that number on real code. This is one small function, and some mutants in a real project can't be killed because they don't change the behavior at all.

Running both in CI

The order matters: the tests write the report, the script reads it, and Stryker runs last because it's the slowest step.

- run: npx vitest run
- run: node scripts/check-spec.mjs
- run: npx stryker run

To make Stryker fail the build, add a threshold to its config. I checked this with a score of 95.65% against a break of 100, and it exits with code 1:

"thresholds": { "break": 80 }

The 80 is a starting point I picked for this post, so adjust it to what your codebase can hold. On a large project, point mutate at the files in the spec's "Files and interfaces" section, and use npx stryker run --incremental, which saves its results to a file and reuses them on the next run.

You can also give the survivors to the agent. Use a fresh session, and make it clear what it can't touch, because deleting the assertion or editing the spec is the fastest way to turn a check green:

These mutants survived Stryker. For each one, find the acceptance
criterion in SPEC.md that should have caught it, and strengthen that
test. Do not edit src/ or SPEC.md. If a stronger test fails because the
code is wrong, stop and tell me which criterion the code doesn't meet.

With Claude Code, you can run the same checks in a Stop hook. A hook blocks only on exit code 2 and the script exits with 1, so the hook command needs to convert it: npx vitest run; node scripts/check-spec.mjs || exit 2. I didn't run this hook in the demo.

What these checks can't tell you

Both checks work from the IDs in the test titles, and nothing verifies that a test labeled AC-2 is about AC-2. A strong test with the wrong label passes both. You still have to read the tests for the criteria that matter most, but the report tells you where to start.

The spec itself can also be wrong or incomplete. If nobody wrote the criterion for 100,000 rows, no script will ask about it. That part happens earlier, when you write and review the spec, and the guide has a full example, the agent interview prompt, and a comparison of Spec Kit, OpenSpec and Kiro.

I've only run this on a small example, so if you've used a mutation score as a CI check on code written by an agent, I'd like to know what threshold held up on a real codebase.

articles.title: Why does setTimeout(0) run after your Promise? The event loop, step by step
articles.description: Here's a small JavaScript puzzle. What order do these letters print...
articles.body_html:
Here's a small JavaScript puzzle. What order do these letters print in?

console.log("A");
setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C"));

async function run() {
  console.log("D");
  await null;
  console.log("E");
}

run();
console.log("F");

Take a guess before you scroll.

.

.

.

The answer is:

A D F C E B

B has a delay of 0, but it prints last. To see why, you need to know four things.

The four pieces

The call stack holds the code running right now. JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time on the main thread, and it finishes the current job before starting another.

Host APIs are provided by the browser or Node, not the JavaScript language. Timers are one example. They wait outside the call stack, so waiting doesn't block your code.

The macrotask queue (also called the task queue) holds jobs such as timer callbacks. The event loop takes one at a time.

The microtask queue holds jobs such as Promise callbacks and the code that continues after an await. It's drained completely before the next macrotask runs.

The event loop is the rule that connects them:

  1. Run the current task until the call stack is empty.
  2. Run every microtask, including any new ones added along the way.
  3. Take one macrotask and run it.
  4. Repeat.

Walking through the code

Step 1: console.log("A"). This is synchronous, so it prints right away.

Output: A

Step 2: setTimeout(..., 0). The timer is handed to the host. Its callback, which prints B, can't run until the current code has finished. It goes into the macrotask queue when the timer expires.

Step 3: Promise.resolve().then(...). The Promise is already fulfilled, so its callback, which prints C, goes straight into the microtask queue. It doesn't run yet, because .then callbacks never run synchronously.

Step 4: run(). Calling an async function runs its body synchronously until the first await. So D prints immediately.

Output: A D

Step 5: await null. This is the part that surprises people. await pauses run and queues the rest of the function, the line that prints E, as a microtask. Control goes back to the code that called run().

Step 6: console.log("F"). This is still the original script, so it prints now.

Output: A D F

Step 7: the call stack is empty. Now the microtask queue is drained, in order. C was queued first, then E.

Output: A D F C E

Step 8: one macrotask runs. The timer callback finally gets its turn.

Output: A D F C E B

What setTimeout(fn, 0) really means

It doesn't mean "run this now." It means "run this in a later task, as soon as possible." The delay is a minimum, not a guarantee.

That matters in real code. If the call stack stays busy, or a long chain of microtasks keeps adding more microtasks, the timer has to wait. In a browser, the page can't repaint during that time either, which is how a page ends up frozen.

Three things to remember

  • Synchronous code always finishes first.
  • All microtasks run before the next macrotask.
  • Code before the first await in an async function runs synchronously. Code after it doesn't.

See it run

Reading this is one thing, but it clicked for me when I could watch the queues change. I built a step-through version of this exact example, where you can watch the call stack, both queues and the console at every step:

Step through the event loop

It's part of Software Atlas, a free site I'm building with interactive explanations of how software works. It has no ads and no sign-up.

articles.title: How nice it is to talk — BeeDialogue lands in BeeEngine 2.11.0
articles.description: Hi. I'm Antonio. I'm 53. I build things out of pure passion.  I don't talk much. But when I do…...
articles.body_html:
Hi. I'm Antonio. I'm 53. I build things out of pure passion.

I don't talk much. But when I do… BeeDialogue comes out.

From “dialogue” to a dialogue plugin

BeeEngine is a small 2D HTML5 Canvas engine I keep shaping in the open. Physics, scenes, sprites, tiles, audio buses, an inventory plugin, a locale plugin. Useful pieces. Quiet pieces.

What was missing for story-shaped games was obvious: a place for NPCs to say something without me inventing a new if tree every weekend.

So v2.11.0 adds BeeDialogue.

Not a chatbot. Not a voice synthesizer. A dialogue tree: speakers, lines, branching choices, straight-line advances. The kind of thing you wire to a blue rectangle that pretends to be a guide on a bridge.

The engine stays blind (on purpose)

BeeEngine has a plugin contract I take seriously. The core does not import plugins. A plugin attaches itself.

import { BeeEngine } from 'beeengine';
import { BeeDialogue, BeeLocale } from 'beeengine/plugins';

const game = new BeeEngine('c', 800, 480);
const locale = new BeeLocale({ /* strings… */, engine: game });

const dialogue = new BeeDialogue({ engine: game, locale, cancelKey: 'Escape' });
// attach() registers it as 'dialogue' — detach() unregisters

No monkey-patch of loop(). No hijacking of update / render. BeeDialogue has no tick of its own and no DOM listeners. Your scene calls the verbs:

  • handleInput(input) from scene.update
  • draw(ctx) from scene.draw (screen space, after the camera)

The motor stays a motor. The plugin stays a plugin. I sleep better.

A tree you can read

You load a tree once. Nodes can be an array (easier to skim) or a map. Literal text / speaker work. Or textKey / speakerKey if you pass an optional BeeLocale (constructor, setLocale, or engine.plugin('locale')).

dialogue.load({
  start: 'intro',
  nodes: [
    {
      id: 'intro',
      speakerKey: 'guide',
      textKey: 'hi',
      choices: [
        { textKey: 'ask_map', next: 'map', data: { topic: 'map' } },
        { textKey: 'bye', next: null, data: { topic: 'bye' } }
      ]
    },
    { id: 'map', speakerKey: 'guide', textKey: 'map', next: 'tip' },
    { id: 'tip', speakerKey: 'guide', textKey: 'tip' }
  ]
});

Rules that saved me from myself:

  • Node without choices → advance() follows next (or ends).
  • Node with choices → choose(index).
  • The wrong verb returns false and warns. Good. I need warnings more than cleverness.
  • start() while already open does a clean restart (end with reason restart, then start again).

Drawing choices (without becoming a second renderer)

BeeDialogue is not BeeText.drawHUD. It draws a simple panel when you ask.

const scene = {
  update(_dt, input) {
    if (input.wasPressed('KeyE') && !dialogue.isOpen()) dialogue.start();
    dialogue.handleInput(input); // Space / Enter advances or confirms; arrows move the highlight
  },
  draw(ctx) {
    dialogue.draw(ctx, { x: 40, width: ctx.canvas.width - 80 });
  }
};

onChange reports start, node, choice, advance, and end (with a reason: finished, cancel, restart, reload, missing-node…). Enough to feed a future quest plugin without hard-wiring anything today.

And yes — toJSON / fromJSON save the tree and where you stood, so you can tuck the DTO into BeeSave next to inventory slots. Definitions stay yours; restore reopens on the saved node and emits node (not a fake second start).

About that demo label

The demo is examples/dialogue.html. Press E.

The English string does not say “E to talk”.

It says “E to interact”.

Because BeeDialogue does not talk. It does not clear its throat. It does not do regional accents. It advances nodes. The joke writes itself, and I left it in the locale table on purpose (talk: 'E to interact'). Press L if you want Italian. The guide still will not speak aloud. She will, however, mention a village east of a bridge, which is already more social than most of my week.

Why this shape

I like small contracts:

Piece Job
BeeLocale t(key) — pure read
BeeInventory stacks, use, equip — no draw loop
BeeDialogue tree state — you draw and feed input

Together they feel like a tiny RPG toolkit without pretending to be one. Next ideas on the shelf (one at a time): Quest, Post FX, scene Transition, action remapping… Lights, Spine, Net later. Those touch more surface area. Dialogue was the polite guest who hangs its coat on attach and leaves with detach.

Try it

  • Repo: BeeEngine-V2.5.0 (package beeengine 2.11.0)
  • Demo: examples/dialogue.html
  • Tests: node scripts/test-beedialogue.mjs
  • Import: import { BeeDialogue } from 'beeengine/plugins'

If you break it, tell me how. If you use it in a jam game with three lines of dialogue and a torch tip, tell me that too. Short messages welcome — I don't talk much.

But when I do… you already know what comes out.

— Antonio
